Cloud Readiness

Old .NET Framework dependency detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
DataLoader/DataLoader.csproj

Explanation

Applications running on frameworks older than .NET Framework 4.8 could have potential compatibility issues.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, run the app on .NET Framework 4.8 (preinstalled) without retargeting if feasible; review runtime breaking changes and validate on Managed Instance staging.

Azure App Service runs apps on .NET Framework 4.8 or .NET Framework 3.5. Upgrade to a newer target framework or double check that your application works correctly when running on .NET Framework 4.8.

Apps that already run on .NET Framework 3.5 or .NET Framework 4.8 do not need changed even if they target an older framework version.

Although retargeting to .NET Framework 4.8 will address this issue, it is not necessary. It is only necessary to ensure that the app runs correctly on .NET Framework 3.5 or .NET Framework 4.8. Applications built against older versions of the .NET Framework can run on newer versions (like 4.8) and the runtime will automatically tweak certain behaviors so that the runtime behaves as much as possible as the targeted version. Breaking change documentation mentions both runtime breaking changes and retargeting breaking changes. Runtime breaking changes refer to differences in behavior when applications are run on a newer version of the .NET Framework. These are the behavioral differences which cannot be tweaked away and will matter for applications migrating to Azure App Service. Retargeting breaking changes are changes which only manifest when an app targets a newer version of the .NET Framework. These should not cause issues during App Service migration scenarios because apps do not need re-targeted.

Actions to address this issue:
1. Review breaking changes between the version of the .NET Framework the application runs on now and .NET Framework 4.8 to make sure none are likely to affect the application.
2. Test the application running on .NET Framework 3.5 or .NET Framework 4.8 to ensure it works as expected.

Architecture Diagram

JobSearch consists of an ASP.NET MVC web application for searching NYC job postings and a separate console utility for loading JSON data into Azure Search.

Data Storage & External Services

The application uses two Azure AI Search indexes, nycjobs and zipcodes, for its searchable data. The web application queries them through the Azure Search .NET SDK; the separate loader creates indexes and uploads schema and JSON files through the Azure Search REST API. No relational database or cache is configured. A Bing geocoding helper package and Bing key setting are present, but no geocoding call was identified in the application source.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • The MVC web application and the data import utility are separate projects with distinct responsibilities.
  • Job searches, suggestions, and record lookups are served as JSON actions and backed by Azure AI Search.
  • Azure Search endpoint and credentials are configured in application settings rather than supplied through dependency injection.

DTOs & Contracts

NYCJob is the search response wrapper containing results, facets, and a count; NYCJobLookup wraps a single Azure Search document for lookup responses. These are mutable C# classes, not immutable records. Search and lookup result content uses Azure Search SDK model types. The DataLoader serializes and deserializes JSON through Newtonsoft.Json. No OpenAPI/Swagger, protobuf, or GraphQL contract was found.

Communication Patterns

Browser-to-web and web-to-Azure Search calls are synchronous. The web application uses the Azure Search .NET SDK; the separate DataLoader uses HttpClient and the Azure Search REST API over HTTPS. No message broker, service discovery, API gateway, client-side load balancing, retry policy, circuit breaker, bulkhead, or explicit timeout configuration was identified. Search exceptions are caught by the search wrapper and return null; callers do not have a defined fallback response.

No API authentication, authorization checks, or TLS enforcement are configured for the MVC endpoints in the application code. The DataLoader and web project use API keys for their outbound Azure Search requests, and the loader constructs an HTTPS service URI.

Core Business Workflows

JobSearch helps users discover New York City job postings by keyword, category, salary, recency, and location. A separate utility provisions the search indexes and loads the job and ZIP-code reference data used by the web experience.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
JobPostingNYCJobsWeb / Job SearchA public-sector job announcement displayed to job seekersUses location data for distance-based search; no stored relationship to a ZIP-code record is declared
ZipCodeNYCJobsWeb / Location SearchGeographic reference record used to resolve a ZIP code to a pointProvides a location point for distance filtering; no relational key is declared

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
NYCJobsWebJob Search and Location SearchNo local persistence; reads job and ZIP-code search documentsAzure AI Search
DataLoaderSearch Data ProvisioningNo local persistence; provisions and uploads source recordsAzure AI Search REST API and repository schema/data files

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Search job postings

  1. A user submits search text and optional title, posting-type, salary, sort, page, and location criteria.
  2. If search text is blank, the web action searches for all postings using *.
  3. The search component builds query options, requested fields, facets, and any supported sorting or filters.
  4. Azure AI Search returns matching postings, facets, and the total count; the web application returns them in a search response.
  5. When a distance limit is requested, the application first looks up the ZIP-code document and uses its coordinates for a geographic filter.

Workflow 2: Suggest search terms and retrieve a job

The suggestion action sends the supplied term to the job index and returns unique suggested terms. The job lookup action retrieves a document by its identifier and wraps it in the lookup response. Both flows depend on the matching document being available in Azure AI Search.

Workflow 3: Load search data

The console utility processes the zipcodes and nycjobs indexes in sequence. For each, it attempts to delete the index, creates it from the corresponding schema file, and uploads matching JSON files. This import flow is an explicit data mutation, not a continuous synchronization process.

Cross-Service Data Flows

The web application reads search data from the Azure AI Search service, while the independent loader provisions and writes to the same service. Job and ZIP-code results are not joined through a relational key: for distance searches the web application performs a ZIP-code lookup, extracts its geographic point, and supplies that point in a subsequent job search. No circuit breaker or fallback data source was identified; if search fails, the search wrapper returns null and the controller may fail while constructing its response.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant User as "Job Seeker" participant Web as "Job Search" participant Search as "Azure AI Search" User->>Web: Search jobs with optional ZIP and distance alt Distance filter requested Web->>Search: Find ZIP-code coordinates Search-->>Web: ZIP-code geographic point else No distance filter Note over Web: Use supplied default or location coordinates end Web->>Search: Search jobs with text, filters, sorting, and facets alt Matching search succeeds Search-->>Web: Job postings, facets, and total count Web-->>User: Display matching jobs else Search operation fails Search-->>Web: Error Note over Web: No business fallback is defined Web-->>User: Request may fail end

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • A blank keyword is treated as a wildcard search for all jobs.
  • Distance filtering is applied only when the requested maximum distance is positive; the ZIP-code index is queried to derive the center point.
  • Search supports title and posting-type facets, salary range filtering, featured scoring, salary ordering, and most-recent ordering.
  • Results are requested in pages of ten and include facets and a total count.
  • Suggestions are deduplicated before being returned.
  • The loader's index workflow deletes an existing index before recreating it and uploading data; there is no identified transaction, rollback, or compensating action.
  • No explicit request validation framework, role-based authorization, business audit trail, or application transaction boundary was identified.

Version & Compatibility Risks

Both projects target .NET Framework 4.5 or 4.7.2, and the package manifests contain older releases of ASP.NET MVC, jQuery, Newtonsoft.Json, and Azure libraries. These versions may present compatibility and support concerns when upgrading to modern .NET; the projects also use legacy packages.config dependency management.

Notable Observations

  • The solution pins two different Newtonsoft.Json versions: 10.0.3 in the web project and 9.0.1 in the loader.
  • The web project references Azure SDK and legacy Microsoft REST client packages together.
  • Several System.* packages support compatibility with the older target frameworks.
  • BingGeocodingHelper is declared by the web project, while its use is not evident from package metadata alone.
